cotton.origin: Cotton fiber grows as seed hairs on shrubs of the genus Gossypium. Cultivars derived from the upland species Gossypium hirsutum supply roughly 90% of world production, typically with staple lengths of about 7/8 to 1 5/16 inches. Gossypium barbadense, native to tropical South America, supplies extra-long staple (ELS) types such as American Pima, which USDA describes as about 1 1/4 to 1 9/16 inches in staple and only about 3 to 5% of the US crop. USDA outlooks track China, India, Brazil, the United States, Pakistan and Australia among the major producers.
cotton.structure: Each fiber is a single elongated plant cell. From the outside in, a mature fiber has a waxy cuticle, a thin primary wall of about 0.5 to 1 micrometer that mixes cellulose with pectins and other non-cellulosic material, a thick secondary wall that makes up roughly 90% or more of the fiber and is built from layered, spirally wound cellulose microfibrils, and a central lumen that holds the dried remains of the cell contents. Overall cellulose content is about 88 to 96.5%. When the boll opens, the tubular cell dries and collapses into a flattened, twisted ribbon. These convolutions, roughly 200 to 300 per inch, help fibers grip one another during spinning.
cotton.process: Seed cotton is harvested by machine or by hand and taken to a gin, where saw or roller gins separate the lint from the seed. Lint is pressed into bales and classed for grade and staple length before sale. At the spinning mill, bales are opened and cleaned, then carded to individualize fibers into a sliver. Combing is an optional step that removes short fibers for finer, smoother yarns. Drawing, roving and ring, rotor or air-jet spinning follow. Woven or knitted greige fabric is then desized, scoured in alkali to remove waxes and pectins, bleached, often mercerized, and dyed or printed. The ginned seed is a separate stream for oil, meal and short linters.
cotton.performance: The hydroxyl groups of cellulose bind water, so cotton absorbs readily, dries slowly and is generally at least as strong wet as dry, unlike regenerated cellulosic fibers. Its elastic recovery is low, which is why untreated cotton wrinkles. It chars and burns rather than melting. The same hydroxyl groups make it receptive to reactive, direct, vat and sulfur dyes. Mercerization, John Mercer's 1844 treatment with sodium hydroxide, swells the fiber and rounds its collapsed cross-section; Horace Lowe showed around 1889 to 1890 that holding the material under tension during treatment produces the familiar luster. Cotton is vulnerable to mildew in damp storage and to degradation by acids.
cotton.identify: Burn tests are indicative only and should be done on small samples with fire precautions. Cotton ignites readily, smells like burning paper and leaves a small amount of soft gray ash with no hard bead. Under a light microscope, the flattened, twisted ribbon with convolutions and a visible lumen is characteristic; mercerized cotton looks rounder with fewer twists. FTIR confirms cellulose but does not by itself separate cotton from linen or viscose. Pima, Egyptian and organic claims cannot be confirmed by routine fiber tests and need documentary chain-of-custody evidence.
cotton.labeling: In the United States, fiber content is disclosed by generic or common name and percentage by weight under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.) and the FTC rules at 16 CFR Part 303. Species or origin terms such as Pima and production claims such as organic are additional representations that must be truthful and substantiated. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 governs fiber names on textile labels. Organic cotton claims are commonly supported by chain-of-custody certification to standards such as GOTS or OCS; a buyer should check that a certificate covers the specific product and supplier.
cotton.past: Eli Whitney applied for a patent on a mechanical cotton gin in Philadelphia in October 1793 and received it on March 14, 1794. By cutting the labor needed to remove seeds from short-staple upland lint, from roughly a pound a day by hand to fifty pounds or more with the machine, the gin made inland upland cotton profitable. As demand rose in the early nineteenth century, cotton cultivation in the US South expanded and so did the plantation system and its demand for enslaved labor to plant and harvest the crop. US cotton exports grew from under 150,000 pounds before the gin to more than 18 million pounds by about 1800.

silk.origin: Most commercial silk comes from the domesticated silkworm Bombyx mori, whose larvae feed on mulberry leaves. Non-mulberry silks come from other moths: tasar from Antheraea species such as A. mylitta and A. proylei, eri from the domesticated Samia ricini, and golden muga from Antheraea assamensis, which is endemic to Assam and confined largely to the Brahmaputra valley. China is by far the largest producer, followed by India, with smaller output from Uzbekistan, Vietnam, Thailand, Brazil and others according to International Sericultural Commission statistics.
silk.structure: A Bombyx mori cocoon is wound from one continuous filament, typically several hundred to about 1,500 m long. Each filament is two fibroin strands (brins) glued together by sericin; fibroin makes up roughly 70 to 80% of cocoon silk and sericin 20 to 30%. Fibroin is assembled from a heavy chain of about 350 kDa, a light chain of about 25 kDa and the P25 glycoprotein in roughly a 6:6:1 ratio. Repeats such as GAGAGS in the heavy chain pack into antiparallel beta-sheet crystallites set in less ordered regions. Degummed brins have a rounded triangular cross-section about 5 to 10 microns wide, which scatters light and gives silk its luster.
silk.process: Larvae spin cocoons at the end of the feeding period. In conventional reeling the pupae are killed by heat or steam (stifling) so the filament stays unbroken. Cocoons are cooked to soften sericin, and the filament ends of several cocoons are reeled together into raw silk, which is then twisted (thrown) into yarn. Degumming, usually by soap or alkali at elevated temperature, hydrolyzes and removes sericin, removing a corresponding share of weight and revealing luster. Waste and pierced cocoons, including eri cocoons left after the moth emerges, are degummed and spun as staple (spun silk).
silk.performance: Silk has a standard moisture regain of about 11%. Dry tenacity is typically cited at about 2.4 to 5.1 g/den, but wetting disrupts hydrogen bonding and strength falls by roughly 15 to 20%, so wet silk should not be wrung. Ultraviolet light breaks hydrogen bonds and then oxidizes and cleaves the polypeptide chains, causing yellowing and strength loss, so silk curtains and linings degrade in sun. Silk takes acid, metal-complex and reactive dyes well. Metallic weighting (historically tin salts) increases drape and weight but accelerates deterioration.
silk.identify: Burn tests are indicative only and should be done with care: silk burns slowly, smells like burning hair and leaves a crushable black bead. Microscopy shows smooth, scale-free filaments with a rounded triangular cross-section; raw silk shows paired brins in a sericin sheath, while wild silks are generally coarser and flatter than mulberry silk. Protein spectroscopy (FTIR) and mass-spectrometric proteomics of fibroin peptides can confirm silk, a method used to detect silk residues in archaeological burials.
silk.labeling: In the US, silk is a natural fiber name under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.) and 16 CFR Part 303. The FTC's 1960 interpretation requiring disclosure of metallically weighted silk (16 CFR 14.4) was repealed effective August 15, 1995; the Commission said misrepresentation remained actionable under Section 5 of the FTC Act. In the EU, silk is an Annex I fiber name in Regulation 1007/2011. Terms like 'peace silk' or 'ahimsa silk' have no statutory definition and need supplier evidence.
silk.past: Mass-spectrometric detection of fibroin peptides in soil from tombs at Jiahu, Henan, published in PLOS One in 2016, is presented as biomolecular evidence of silk use about 8,500 years ago. The earliest known silk fabric fragments, more than 4,700 years old, come from Qianshanyang in Zhejiang, a Liangzhu culture site. According to Procopius, monks returning from the east brought silkworms to Constantinople for the emperor Justinian I in the mid-sixth century CE, founding a Byzantine silk industry that dominated European production for centuries.
